Solid harmonics, vector harmonics and the Lamé solutions ​

This page defines the complex solid harmonics that expand a harmonic field about a point, the vector harmonics and the displacements of an isotropic elastic solid built on them, the formulas that carry each family from one center to another, and their sums over a periodic array. The meridian parts of the same harmonics in the spherical chart are those of Spheroidal harmonics and their re-expansion; here they are written with their azimuthal factor and in the normalization in which the translation formulas have no other factor than the harmonics themselves (Kushch, 2013).

a harmonic whose order exceeds its degree being zero. The series converges in the ball about the second center that reaches the first one.

6. Periodic arrays ​

On a periodic array of sources the decaying harmonics are replaced by their sums over the images. The sum of the harmonics of degree 2, which decrease as , converges only conditionally, a difficulty met by Lord Rayleigh (1892) and settled by McPhedran and McKenzie (1978) for the simple cubic array. It is avoided by starting from a function periodic by construction: the potential of a unit source repeated on the lattice of periods , at the points , neutralized by a uniform background (Hasimoto, 1959),

A decaying harmonic is a derivative of ,   with         a harmonic polynomial of the partial derivatives, and its periodic counterpart is  , computed by lattice_solid_harmonics. is split as Ewald (1921) did, with a parameter ,

running over the reciprocal lattice, and the derivative goes through each sum term by term. On a radial function a harmonic polynomial of the derivatives acts as     , which gives   , with   and      ; on a plane wave it multiplies by . Both sums converge as a Gaussian at every degree, and their truncation follows the precision of the number type. At a lattice point the source of that point is left out,   being regular there.

The background has one consequence.
